Reconstructing a finite helical worldtube\n\nUse native Euclidean four-dimensional coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nwith metric\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds^2=dw^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine a finite helical centerline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nt\\\\\nR[\\cos(kt)-1]\\\\\nR\\sin(kt)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\qquad -T\\le t\\le T.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe translation by \\(-R\\) merely places the centerline at the spatial origin when \\(t=0\\).\n\nIt does not alter the intrinsic geometry.\n\nHere \\(R\\) is the coil radius, \\(k\\) is angular winding per unit longitudinal coordinate, and \\(T\\) is the half-length of the modeled history.\n\n## Tangent and curvature\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\nh'(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\\n-Rk\\sin(kt)\\\\\nRk\\cos(kt)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts squared norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|h'(t)\\|^2=1+R^2k^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tan\\theta_4=Rk.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second derivative is\n\n\\[\nh''(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\\n-Rk^2\\cos(kt)\\\\\n-Rk^2\\sin(kt)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nh'\\cdot h''=0,\n\\]\n\nthe Euclidean four-dimensional curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_4=\n\\frac{Rk^2}{1+R^2k^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis already reveals something useful.\n\nTwo helices can have identical\n\n\\[\nRk\n\\]\n\nand therefore identical \\(\\theta_4\\), while having different\n\n\\[\nRk^2.\n\\]\n\nTheir local tangents agree, but their curvatures do not.\n\nWe can test whether finite-core slicing detects that distinction.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact finite-core intersection\n\nDefine the solid worldtube of intrinsic radius \\(\\epsilon\\) as the Euclidean radius-\\(\\epsilon\\) neighborhood of the finite centerline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_\\epsilon=\n\\left\\{\nX:\n\\min_{-T\\le t\\le T}\n\\|X-h(t)\\|\n\\le\\epsilon\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an explicit geometric model.\n\nIt is not yet a Kerr shell, hollow filament, or physically derived particle structure.\n\nNow intersect it with the timesheet\n\n\\[\nw=0.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nq=(x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nc(t)=\n\\left(\nR[\\cos(kt)-1],\nR\\sin(kt),\n0\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nThe squared four-dimensional distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2=t^2+\\|q-c(t)\\|^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a point to belong to the slice, there must exist a parameter \\(t\\) satisfying\n\n\\[\nt^2+\\|q-c(t)\\|^2\\le\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\|q-c(t)\\|^2\\le\\epsilon^2-t^2.\n\\]\n\nThis requires\n\n\\[\n|t|\\le\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nCombining that with the finite centerline domain gives the exact result:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(S_\\epsilon)=\n\\bigcup_{|t|\\le\\min(T,\\epsilon)}\nB_3\n\\left(\nc(t),\n\\sqrt{\\epsilon^2-t^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\n**The timesheet intersection is a union of three-dimensional balls whose centers move along a restricted section of the helix.**\n\nThat is the central geometrical result.\n\nIt follows directly from the specified four-dimensional distance.\n\nNo additional interaction law was introduced.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The local straight-tube approximation\n\nFor sufficiently small \\(\\epsilon\\), the helix can be approximated by its tangent at the intersection point.\n\nAt \\(t=0\\),\n\n\\[\nh'(0)=\n(1,0,Rk,0).\n\\]\n\nThe straight-tube approximation has semiaxes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\n\\epsilon,\n\\epsilon,\n\\epsilon\\sqrt{1+R^2k^2}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe elongated direction is tangent to the projected spatial motion.\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\mathrm{long}}=\n\\epsilon\\sec\\theta_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis reproduces the earlier straight-tube slicing result under BR-005's angle convention.\n\nBut it is only the tangent approximation.\n\nIt discards the centerline's curvature and finite winding.\n\nThe exact union-of-balls construction retains both.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Minimal-pair experiment\n\nI constructed two helices with identical initial position and tangent.\n\nTheir parameters are:\n\n| Parameter | Helix A | Helix B |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| \\(R\\) | 2 | 1 |\n| \\(k\\) | \\(\\pi\\) | \\(2\\pi\\) |\n| \\(Rk\\) | \\(2\\pi\\) | \\(2\\pi\\) |\n| \\(\\epsilon\\) | 0.25 | 0.25 |\n| \\(T\\) | 1 | 1 |\n| \\(\\theta_4\\) | 80.956939° | 80.956939° |\n\nBoth have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh(0)=(0,0,0,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh'(0)=(1,0,2\\pi,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nTheir local straight-tube approximations are identical.\n\nNevertheless, their curvatures differ:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_{4,A}=0.487647738484071\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_{4,B}=0.975295476968142.\n}\n\\]\n\nHelix B has exactly twice the four-dimensional curvature of A.\n\n## Exact intersection results\n\nThe executed calculation gives:\n\n| Quantity | Helix A | Helix B |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Minimum slice \\(x\\) | −0.613845592402 | −1.019771197194 |\n| Maximum slice \\(y\\) | 1.441751640768 | 1.104231402918 |\n| Straight-tube predicted \\(y\\) half-width | 1.590566282892 | 1.590566282892 |\n\nThe difference in the negative \\(x\\)-extent is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta x_{\\min}\n=-0.405925604792.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe difference in the positive \\(y\\)-extent is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta y_{\\max}\n=-0.337520237850.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are substantial geometric differences despite identical first-order tangent data.\n\n### Class P: actual intersections\n\n![Exact finite-core helical slice comparison](sandbox:/mnt/data/kestrel_s4_20261019/finite_helix_minimal_pair_classP.png)\n\nThe dotted contour is the shared tangent approximation.\n\nThe two other contours are calculated from the full finite-core intersections.\n\n**The instantaneous tangent does not determine the complete finite-core slice.**\n\nCurvature and winding remain geometrically distinguishable.\n\nThis is a concrete example of the representational information loss discussed in ND-2026-10-18-04.\n\n---\n\n# 6. A second result: slicing and convexification do not commute\n\nND-2026-10-18-07 explicitly asks whether structural coarse-graining and timesheet intersection can be exchanged without changing the result.\n\nWe can answer that question for one precisely defined coarse-graining operator.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nC_4\n\\]\n\ndenote convexification in four-dimensional Euclidean space.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nP\n\\]\n\ndenote intersection with the timesheet \\(w=0\\).\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nC_3\n\\]\n\ndenote convexification of the resulting three-dimensional set.\n\nThe question is whether\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(C_4(S_\\epsilon))\n\\stackrel{?}{=}\nC_3(P(S_\\epsilon)).\n}\n\\]\n\n## An exact counterexample\n\nUse Helix A:\n\n\\[\nR=2,\\qquad k=\\pi,\\qquad T=1,\\qquad\\epsilon=0.25.\n\\]\n\nAt the two centerline endpoints,\n\n\\[\nt=-1,\\quad t=+1,\n\\]\n\nthe spatial \\(x\\)-coordinate is\n\n\\[\nx=2[\\cos(\\pm\\pi)-1].\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{x=-4.}\n\\]\n\nThe two endpoints have opposite \\(w\\)-coordinates.\n\nTheir midpoint is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(0,-4,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause this point is a convex combination of two points in the original tube,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(0,-4,0,0)\\in C_4(S_\\epsilon).\n}\n\\]\n\nIt also lies in the timesheet \\(w=0\\).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(-4,0,0)\\in P(C_4(S_\\epsilon)).\n}\n\\]\n\nNow examine the opposite order.\n\nFor every point in the original timesheet slice,\n\n\\[\n|t|\\le\\epsilon=0.25.\n\\]\n\nIts \\(x\\)-coordinate obeys\n\n\\[\nx\\ge\nR[\\cos(kt)-1]-\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n|kt|\\le\\frac\\pi4,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx\\ge\n2\\left(\\cos\\frac\\pi4-1\\right)-0.25.\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx\\ge-0.835786437626905.\n}\n\\]\n\nConvexification within the timesheet preserves this lower bound.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(-4,0,0)\\notin C_3(P(S_\\epsilon)).\n}\n\\]\n\nWe have proved\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(C_4(S_\\epsilon))\n\\ne\nC_3(P(S_\\epsilon)).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe certified separation along \\(x\\) is at least\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n3.16421356237309.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact geometrical counterexample, not merely a numerical discrepancy.\n\n### Interpretation boundary\n\nConvexification is only one possible coarse-graining operation.\n\nThis calculation does not prove that physical worldtubes are convexified, or that this difference corresponds to an experimentally measurable interaction.\n\nIt demonstrates that **the order of representation-changing operations can matter**.\n\nA physically justified smoothing or aggregation operator must therefore be specified before its relationship to timesheet intersection can be assumed.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Topology and limiting cases\n\nThe exact slice is path-connected.\n\nEach ball in the union is connected, and its center lies on the continuous projected centerline segment. Every point in a ball can be connected to that center, and the centers form a continuous path within the union.\n\nThe executed numerical grid also returned one connected component for each fixture.\n\nThe limiting cases were checked.\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\nk\\to0,\n\\]\n\nthe helix becomes a straight time-directed centerline.\n\nThe timesheet slice becomes the ordinary three-dimensional ball of radius \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nThe same result follows when\n\n\\[\nR\\to0.\n\\]\n\nAs\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon\\to0,\n\\]\n\nthe rescaled exact intersection approaches the tangent-line ellipsoid.\n\nFor Helix A, the predicted limiting elongated semiaxis ratio is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sqrt{1+(2\\pi)^2}\n=\n6.362265131567328.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe executed results are:\n\n| \\(\\epsilon\\) | Calculated ratio |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0.01 | 6.361269716917457 |\n| 0.001 | 6.362255176770700 |\n| 0.0001 | 6.362265032019296 |\n\nThe numerical sequence approaches the predicted tangent limit.\n\n### Dimensional consistency\n\nThe quantities \\(R,T,\\epsilon,t,w,x,y,z\\) have dimensions of length.\n\nThe winding rate \\(k\\) and curvature \\(\\kappa_4\\) have dimensions of inverse length.\n\nThe quantities \\(Rk\\) and \\(\\theta_4\\) are dimensionless.\n\nAll distance and intersection inequalities are dimensionally homogeneous.\n\n---\n\n# 8. The geometric question\n\nMeridian's preceding calculation established that two opposite-handed helices can have the same coarse-grained centerline while retaining different signed winding.\n\nThat construction also has an interesting finite-core consequence.\n\nSuppose two constituent worldlines are separated by \\(2a\\) at every simultaneous parameter value.\n\nDoes that guarantee that their finite-radius four-dimensional worldtubes are disjoint?\n\n**No.**\n\nThe reason is that the closest point on one worldline need not occur at the same parameter value as the closest point on the other.\n\nWe must minimize distance across the complete histories.\n\nThis is a geometrical admissibility calculation, not an invented force law.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact double-helix construction\n\nWork in native Euclidean four-space with coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z).\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_+(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\npt\\\\\na\\cos\\omega t\\\\\na\\sin\\omega t\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_-(s)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nps\\\\\n-a\\cos\\omega s\\\\\n-a\\sin\\omega s\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe parameters \\(p\\) and \\(a\\) have dimensions of length.\n\nThe history parameters \\(t,s\\) are dimensionless.\n\nThe angular frequency \\(\\omega\\) is measured in radians per parameter unit.\n\nThe squared Euclidean distance between the two points is\n\n\\[\nD^2(t,s)=\n\\|X_+(t)-X_-(s)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\nD^2(t,s)\n=\np^2(t-s)^2\n+\na^2(\\cos\\omega t+\\cos\\omega s)^2\n+\na^2(\\sin\\omega t+\\sin\\omega s)^2.\n\\]\n\nUse the trigonometric identity\n\n\\[\n(\\cos A+\\cos B)^2+\n(\\sin A+\\sin B)^2\n=\n4\\cos^2\\left(\\frac{A-B}{2}\\right).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD^2(t,s)\n=\np^2(t-s)^2+\n4a^2\\cos^2\n\\left(\n\\frac{\\omega(t-s)}2\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{LOOM-01}\n\\]\n\nThis identity was independently verified symbolically.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Simultaneous separation is insufficient\n\nFor simultaneous points,\n\n\\[\nt=s.\n\\]\n\nEquation LOOM-01 becomes\n\n\\[\nD^2(t,t)=4a^2.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD(t,t)=2a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is the instantaneous centerline separation.\n\nBut the minimum distance between the complete worldlines is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}\n=\n\\min_{t,s}\\|X_+(t)-X_-(s)\\|.\n}\n\\]\n\nThere is no general reason for this minimum to occur at \\(t=s\\).\n\nIndeed, it often does not.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\delta=|t-s|\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nx=|\\omega|\\delta.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD^2(x)=\n\\frac{p^2}{\\omega^2}x^2+\n4a^2\\cos^2(x/2).\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the dimensionless parameter\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nk=\\frac{a|\\omega|}{p}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis produces two distinct geometric regimes.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact clearance threshold\n\n## Regime I: \\(k\\le1\\)\n\nRewrite the squared distance as\n\n\\[\nD^2(\\delta)\n=\n4a^2+\np^2\\delta^2-\n4a^2\\sin^2(\\omega\\delta/2).\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n|\\sin u|\\le|u|,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nD^2(\\delta)\n\\ge\n4a^2+\n(p^2-a^2\\omega^2)\\delta^2.\n\\]\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\na|\\omega|\\le p,\n\\]\n\nthe second term is nonnegative.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=2a.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn this regime, simultaneous separation correctly identifies the global closest approach.\n\n## Regime II: \\(k>1\\)\n\nDifferentiate the squared distance:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dD^2}{dx}\n=\n2\\frac{p^2}{\\omega^2}x\n-\n2a^2\\sin x.\n\\]\n\nAt a stationary point,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{p^2}{\\omega^2}x\n=\na^2\\sin x.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=k^2\\sin x.\n}\n\\tag{LOOM-02}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(k>1\\), this equation has exactly one positive root in\n\n\\[\n0<x<\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThis follows because \\(\\sin x/x\\) decreases strictly from 1 to 0 on that interval.\n\nAt \\(x=0\\), the quadratic coefficient in the expansion of \\(D^2\\) is negative.\n\nTherefore, \\(x=0\\) is not the minimum.\n\nFor \\(x\\ge\\pi\\),\n\n\\[\nD^2(x)\n\\ge\n\\frac{p^2\\pi^2}{\\omega^2}\n=\nD^2(\\pi).\n\\]\n\nThe interior minimum lies below \\(D^2(\\pi)\\).\n\nThus the unique root \\(x_*\\in(0,\\pi)\\) gives the global minimum.\n\nWe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=\n\\sqrt{\n\\frac{p^2}{\\omega^2}x_*^2+\n4a^2\\cos^2(x_*/2)\n}.\n}\n\\tag{LOOM-03}\n\\]\n\nFor finite histories, this formula remains exact whenever the allowed parameter interval admits\n\n\\[\n|t-s|=\\frac{x_*}{|\\omega|}.\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 6. Finite-core nonintersection\n\nDefine the Euclidean radius-\\(\\epsilon\\) neighborhood of a centerline \\(G\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_\\epsilon(G)=\n\\{X\\in\\mathbb R^4:d_4(X,G)\\le\\epsilon\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsider the two finite-core worldtubes\n\n\\[\nC_\\epsilon(X_+)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nC_\\epsilon(X_-).\n\\]\n\nTheir interiors remain separated when\n\n\\[\n2\\epsilon<D_{\\min}.\n\\]\n\nAt equality, their boundaries first touch.\n\nFor larger radii, they overlap.\n\nThus the exact disjointness criterion for these closed distance neighborhoods is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2\\epsilon<D_{\\min}.\n}\n\\tag{LOOM-04}\n\\]\n\nThis is stronger than the simultaneous-separation condition\n\n\\[\n2\\epsilon<2a.\n\\]\n\nWhen \\(k>1\\),\n\n\\[\nD_{\\min}<2a.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, there exists a range of core radii satisfying\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{D_{\\min}}2<\\epsilon<a.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn that range, the simultaneous cross-sections suggest separation, while the complete four-dimensional neighborhoods intersect.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Numerical fixture\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\np=1,\n\\qquad\na=0.25,\n\\qquad\n\\omega=2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nUse finite histories\n\n\\[\n-\\frac12\\le t,s\\le\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe dimensionless ratio is\n\n\\[\nk=\\frac{\\pi}{2}\n=\n1.5707963267948966\\ldots\n\\]\n\nSince \\(k>1\\), the closest approach occurs at unequal history parameters.\n\nSolving LOOM-02 gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_*=2.1132246218111611188838328930706750341108\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_*=\n0.3363301444247474\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nThe resulting minimum distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}=\n0.4166423053559051461209250176194687068627\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{critical}}\n=\n0.2083211526779525730604625088097343534313\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nCompare this with the simultaneous estimate:\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{simultaneous}}=a=0.25.\n\\]\n\nThe actual critical radius is approximately **16.67% smaller**.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Explicit timesheet intersection witness\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0.22.\n\\]\n\nAt every simultaneous parameter value, the centerlines are separated by\n\n\\[\n2a=0.5.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n2\\epsilon=0.44<0.5,\n\\]\n\ntwo three-dimensional balls of radius \\(0.22\\), centered on the simultaneous strand positions, are disjoint.\n\nBut the four-dimensional worldtubes overlap.\n\nTake the closest pair at\n\n\\[\nt=\\frac{\\delta_*}{2},\n\\qquad\ns=-\\frac{\\delta_*}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding centerline points are\n\n\\[\nX_+(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0.1681650722123737\\\\\n0.12295613502740711\\\\\n0.21767358328268047\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nX_-(s)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-0.1681650722123737\\\\\n-0.12295613502740711\\\\\n0.21767358328268047\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nTheir midpoint is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\\n0\\\\\n0.21767358328268047\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNotice that\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{w(M)=0.}\n\\]\n\nThe midpoint lies directly on the timesheet.\n\nIts distance to either selected four-dimensional centerline point is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_4(M,X_\\pm)=0.2083211526779526.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nd_4(M,X_\\pm)<0.22.\n\\]\n\nSo \\(M\\) belongs to both four-dimensional thickened worldtubes.\n\nBut the simultaneous centerline intersections at \\(w=0\\) are\n\n\\[\n(+0.25,0,0)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n(-0.25,0,0).\n\\]\n\nThe three-dimensional distance from \\(M\\) to either is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_3=0.331484221131447.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n0.331484221131447>0.22,\n\\]\n\n\\(M\\) belongs to neither three-dimensional ball constructed after slicing.\n\nHence we have an explicit witness for the failure of simultaneous slice geometry to capture the complete finite-core intersection.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Exact slice construction\n\nAt a fixed history parameter \\(t\\), the centerline point is\n\n\\[\nH(t)=\n(pt,a\\cos\\omega t,a\\sin\\omega t,0).\n\\]\n\nFor a point on the timesheet to lie within distance \\(\\epsilon\\) of this centerline point, its three-dimensional distance from the transverse center must satisfy\n\n\\[\nr^2+p^2t^2\\le\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr(t)=\n\\sqrt{\\epsilon^2-p^2t^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe allowed history interval is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|t|\\le\\frac{\\epsilon}{p}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the exact timesheet intersection is the union of three-dimensional balls centered at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(t)=\n(a\\cos\\omega t,a\\sin\\omega t,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nwith radii\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr(t)=\\sqrt{\\epsilon^2-p^2t^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is not generally a single ball or ellipsoid.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Recovering the straight-tangent ellipse\n\nAt \\(t=0\\),\n\n\\[\nH'(0)=\n(p,0,a\\omega,0).\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nv=a\\omega.\n\\]\n\nA nearby timesheet point can be written as\n\n\\[\nq=(0,a+u,y,z).\n\\]\n\nThe squared distance to the tangent line is\n\n\\[\nD^2(t)\n=\np^2t^2+u^2+(y-vt)^2+z^2.\n\\]\n\nMinimizing with respect to \\(t\\),\n\n\\[\n\\frac{\\partial D^2}{\\partial t}\n=\n2(p^2+v^2)t-2vy=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nt_*=\n\\frac{vy}{p^2+v^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}^2\n=\nu^2+z^2+\n\\frac{p^2}{p^2+v^2}y^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe tangent-line tube intersects the timesheet in an ellipsoid with semiaxes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon,\\quad\n\\epsilon,\\quad\n\\epsilon\\sqrt{1+\\frac{v^2}{p^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing the operative departure angle\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4=\n\\arctan\\frac{|v|}{p},\n\\]\n\nthe third semiaxis becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{tangential}}\n=\n\\epsilon\\sec\\theta_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is consistent with BEDROCK's straight-oblique-core result, with its angle measured from the timesheet rather than from the time normal.\n\n**But this ellipse is exact only for the straight tangent construction.**\n\nThe curved helix has a different exact boundary.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Exact curved-helix envelope\n\nRestrict attention to the \\(z=0\\) plane within the timesheet.\n\nEach contributing disk has center\n\n\\[\nc(t)=\n(a\\cos\\omega t,a\\sin\\omega t)\n\\]\n\nand radius\n\n\\[\nr(t)=\n\\sqrt{\\epsilon^2-p^2t^2}.\n\\]\n\nIts boundary satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\|q-c(t)\\|^2\n=\n\\epsilon^2-p^2t^2.\n\\]\n\nThe envelope condition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(q-c(t))\\cdot c'(t)=p^2t.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the rotating basis\n\n\\[\ne_r=\n(\\cos\\omega t,\\sin\\omega t)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\ne_t=\n(-\\sin\\omega t,\\cos\\omega t).\n\\]\n\nFor \\(v=a\\omega>0\\), the two envelope branches are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nq_\\pm(t)\n={}&c(t)\n+\\frac{p^2t}{v}e_t\\\\\n&\\pm\n\\sqrt{\n\\epsilon^2-p^2t^2\n-\\left(\\frac{p^2t}{v}\\right)^2\n}\\;e_r.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe real-envelope parameter interval is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|t|\n\\le\n\\frac{\\epsilon v}\n{p\\sqrt{p^2+v^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis gives the actual curved footprint, rather than simply extrapolating the straight-tangent ellipse.\n\n---\n\n# 10. 1001)\n\n    vals = np.array([\n        distance_squared(float(t),x,y,z)\n        for t in ts\n    ])\n\n    candidates = [\n        (vals[0],ts[0]),\n        (vals[-1],ts[-1])\n    ]\n\n    for j in bounds=(ts[j-1],ts[j+1]),\n                method='bounded',\n                options={'xatol':1e-14}\n            )\n            candidates.append((result.fun,result.x))\n\n    return W*t\n\n            er = np.array([\n                math.cos(phase),\n                math.sin(phase)\n            ])\n\n            et = np.array([\n                -math.sin(phase),\n                math.cos(phase)\n            ])\n\n            tang = P*P*t/V\n\n            radial = math.sqrt(max(\n                0.0,\n                eps**2-P*P*t*t-tang*tang\n            ))\n\n            q = nearest(A,actual,eps)[0]-eps**2\n    ) < 1e-10\n\n    ts,branches = envelope(eps,121)\n\n    errors = []\n\n    for branch in branches:\n        for i in np.linspace(\n            0,len(branch)-1,11\n Exact equivalence of finite-core constructions\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nH:\\mathbb R\\rightarrow\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nbe a proper, continuously differentiable, regular curve.\n\nDefine its Euclidean radius-\\(\\epsilon\\) neighborhood:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_\\epsilon=\n\\left\\{\nq\\in\\mathbb R^4:\n\\inf_t\\|q-H(t)\\|\\le\\epsilon\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\tag{TERN-01}\n\\]\n\nNow define the complete normal-ball sweep:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nN_\\epsilon=\n\\left\\{\nH(t)+n:\nn\\cdot H'(t)=0,\\quad\n\\|n\\|\\le\\epsilon\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\tag{TERN-02}\n\\]\n\nThe normal space of a regular curve in four-dimensional Euclidean space is three-dimensional.\n\nTherefore, each constituent normal ball is three-dimensional.\n\n## Theorem\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_\\epsilon=N_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\tag{TERN-03}\n\\]\n\n### Proof\n\nFirst, consider any point\n\n\\[\nq=H(t)+n\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nn\\cdot H'(t)=0,\n\\qquad\n\\|n\\|\\le\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nIts distance to the complete centerline cannot exceed its distance to the particular point \\(H(t)\\).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\inf_s\\|q-H(s)\\|\n\\le\n\\|n\\|\n\\le\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{N_\\epsilon\\subseteq T_\\epsilon.}\n\\]\n\nFor the reverse inclusion, choose\n\n\\[\nq\\in T_\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(H\\) is proper, the distance from \\(q\\) to the centerline attains its minimum at some parameter \\(t_*\\).\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nf(t)=\\|q-H(t)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nAt an interior minimum,\n\n\\[\nf'(t_*)=0.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiating,\n\n\\[\nf'(t)=\n-2(q-H(t))\\cdot H'(t).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(q-H(t_*))\\cdot H'(t_*)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe displacement from the nearest centerline point is perpendicular to the tangent.\n\nIts length is at most \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nThus\n\n\\[\nq\\in N_\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_\\epsilon\\subseteq N_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nCombining the inclusions,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_\\epsilon=N_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis equality does not require the normal-coordinate representation to be injective.\n\nThat qualification becomes important below.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The Calder fourth-harmonic fixture\n\nRetain the preceding relay's synthetic construction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_b(t)=\n\\left(\nt,\na\\cos\\omega t,\na\\sin\\omega t,\nb(\\cos2\\omega t-1)\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{TERN-04}\n\\]\n\nUse\n\n\\[\na=0.25,\\qquad\nb=0.10,\\qquad\n\\omega=2\\pi,\\qquad\n\\epsilon=0.30.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_b'(t)=\n\\left(\n1,\n-a\\omega\\sin\\omega t,\na\\omega\\cos\\omega t,\n-2b\\omega\\sin2\\omega t\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{TERN-05}\n\\]\n\nIts squared norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|H_b'(t)\\|^2\n=\n1+a^2\\omega^2+\n4b^2\\omega^2\\sin^2(2\\omega t).\n}\n\\tag{TERN-06}\n\\]\n\nThis expression was checked symbolically.\n\nThe curve is proper because its first coordinate is \\(w=t\\).\n\nTherefore the equivalence theorem applies globally.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Explicit normal-coordinate witness\n\nConsider the timesheet point\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=(0,0.25,0,-0.304).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the original \\(b=0\\) trajectory, the minimum four-dimensional distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd(q,H_0)=0.304.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n0.304>0.30,\n\\]\n\nthe point lies outside the finite-core neighborhood.\n\nFor \\(b=0.10\\), numerical minimization gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd(q,H_{0.10})\n=\n0.296989260481316.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis lies inside the radius-\\(0.30\\) neighborhood.\n\nOne nearest centerline parameter is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nt_*=-0.081898104305913.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding displacement vector is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0.08189810430591257\\\\\n0.03237524127505326\\\\\n0.12304253081722888\\\\\n-0.2555537139522921\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|n\\|=0.296989260481316.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe computed normality residual is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn\\cdot H_b'(t_*)\n=\n-2.04\\times10^{-16}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe residual is consistent with floating-point roundoff.\n\nThus \\(q\\) lies in the normal ball based at \\(t_*\\).\n\nBut \\(q\\) is outside the instantaneous spatial ball centered at \\(H_b(0)\\), because its spatial distance from that center is \\(0.304\\).\n\nThis demonstrates that the complete normal-ball sweep reproduces the cross-temporal geometry that an instantaneous-centerline construction misses.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The geometrical distinction\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nH:\\mathbb R\\rightarrow\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nbe a proper, regular, continuously differentiable curve.\n\nDefine its complete Euclidean radius-\\(\\epsilon\\) neighborhood:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_\\epsilon=\n\\left\\{\nq:\n\\min_t\\|q-H(t)\\|\\le\\epsilon\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-01}\n\\]\n\nDefine the complete swept normal-sphere set:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_\\epsilon=\n\\left\\{\nH(t)+n:\nn\\cdot H'(t)=0,\\quad\n\\|n\\|=\\epsilon\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-02}\n\\]\n\nEach normal sphere is a two-dimensional sphere inside the three-dimensional normal space of the centerline.\n\nSweeping these spheres along the curve produces a three-dimensional immersed set.\n\nThe important question is whether this swept set equals the boundary of the solid distance neighborhood.\n\n## Theorem\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial T_\\epsilon\\subseteq S_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nHowever,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial T_\\epsilon\\ne S_\\epsilon\n}\n\\]\n\nin general.\n\n### Proof of inclusion\n\nTake\n\n\\[\nq\\in\\partial T_\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nFor a proper regular curve, a nearest centerline point exists.\n\nLet its parameter be \\(t_*\\).\n\nSince \\(q\\) lies on the boundary,\n\n\\[\n\\|q-H(t_*)\\|=\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nMinimizing squared distance gives\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d}{dt}\n\\|q-H(t)\\|^2\n\\bigg|_{t=t_*}\n=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(q-H(t_*))\\cdot H'(t_*)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe displacement is normal to the centerline and has length exactly \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nHence\n\n\\[\nq\\in S_\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nThis establishes the inclusion.\n\nThe reverse inclusion fails whenever a point lying on one constituent normal sphere is closer than \\(\\epsilon\\) to another centerline point.\n\nWe can demonstrate that failure explicitly.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The four-dimensional minimal pair\n\nRetain Calder's synthetic fourth-harmonic fixture:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_b(t)=\n\\left(\nt,\na\\cos\\omega t,\na\\sin\\omega t,\nb(\\cos2\\omega t-1)\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-03}\n\\]\n\nThis is a derived mathematical test fixture, not a recovered historical SAT equation.\n\nCompare\n\n\\[\nb=0\n\\]\n\nagainst\n\n\\[\nb>0.\n\\]\n\nAt \\(t=0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_b(0)=(0,a,0,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_b'(0)=(1,0,a\\omega,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth are independent of \\(b\\).\n\nThe instantaneous centerline crossing and tangent therefore remain unchanged.\n\nThe fourth-coordinate harmonic changes the higher-order geometry.\n\n---\n\n# 4. An exact shell witness\n\nChoose the point\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_\\epsilon=(0,a,0,-\\epsilon).\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-04}\n\\]\n\nAt \\(t=0\\), its displacement from the centerline is\n\n\\[\nn=(0,0,0,-\\epsilon).\n\\]\n\nIts length is\n\n\\[\n\\|n\\|=\\epsilon.\n\\]\n\nIts dot product with the tangent is\n\n\\[\nn\\cdot H_b'(0)=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_\\epsilon\\in S_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is true for every positive \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nBut is it on the exterior boundary of the solid tube?\n\nCalculate its distance to the complete four-dimensional history.\n\n\\[\nD^2(t;q_\\epsilon)\n=\n\\|q_\\epsilon-H_b(t)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD^2(t;q_\\epsilon)=\nt^2+\n4a^2\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{\\omega t}{2}\\right)\n+\n\\left(\n\\epsilon-2b\\sin^2\\omega t\n\\right)^2.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-05}\n\\]\n\nAt \\(t=0\\),\n\n\\[\nD^2(0;q_\\epsilon)=\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nBut another history parameter may give a smaller distance.\n\nThat possibility is what distinguishes the swept shell from the exterior boundary.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Derive the local focal threshold\n\nExpand RAVEL-05 around \\(t=0\\).\n\n\\[\nD^2(t;q_\\epsilon)\n=\n\\epsilon^2+c_2t^2+c_4t^4+O(t^6).\n\\]\n\nThe quadratic coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_2=\n1+a^2\\omega^2-4b\\epsilon\\omega^2.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-06}\n\\]\n\nThe quartic coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_4=\n\\omega^4\n\\left(\n-\\frac{a^2}{12}\n+\\frac{4b\\epsilon}{3}\n+4b^2\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-07}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\nc_2<0,\n\\]\n\nthen sufficiently small nonzero \\(t\\) satisfies\n\n\\[\nD^2(t;q_\\epsilon)<\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore \\(q_\\epsilon\\) lies strictly inside the solid tube.\n\nSolving \\(c_2=0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n=\n\\frac{1+a^2\\omega^2}\n{4b\\omega^2}.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-08}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(b>0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon>\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n\\Longrightarrow\nq_\\epsilon\\in\n\\operatorname{int}(T_\\epsilon)\n\\cap S_\\epsilon.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-09}\n\\]\n\nThis proves that the swept normal-sphere set can contain interior points.\n\nThe threshold is local and directional. It is not automatically the global reach of the curve.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Geometric interpretation of the threshold\n\nThe second derivative of the centerline at \\(t=0\\) is\n\n\\[\nH_b''(0)=\n\\left(\n0,\n-a\\omega^2,\n0,\n-4b\\omega^2\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nThe squared tangent norm is\n\n\\[\n\\|H_b'(0)\\|^2=\n1+a^2\\omega^2.\n\\]\n\nThe normal curvature toward the negative \\(z\\)-direction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_{-z}\n=\n\\frac{4b\\omega^2}\n{1+a^2\\omega^2}.\n}\n\\tag{RAVEL-10}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n=\n\\frac1{\\kappa_{-z}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe threshold is the focal distance associated with that normal direction.\n\nThis gives a geometrical explanation for the shell-boundary discrepancy.\n\nWhen the radius exceeds this local focal distance, the normal-sphere sweep folds through the interior of the distance neighborhood.\n\nNo additional force or interaction is required to produce the effect.\n\n---\n\n# 7. First correction: the four-dimensional Green function\n\nThe historical source defines the Laplace-Beltrami operator as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_g=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt g}\n\\partial_A\n\\left(\n\\sqrt g\\,g^{AB}\\partial_B\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nIt then requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_gG_{\\mathrm{top}}(X,X')\n=\n\\delta^{(4)}(X-X').\n}\n\\]\n\nFor flat Euclidean four-space, it proposes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{archived}}(r)=\n\\frac1{4\\pi^2r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The sign is incorrect for the operator and source convention explicitly stated.**\n\nFor a radial function in four dimensions,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4f=f''+\\frac3r f'.\n\\]\n\nAway from the origin,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4(r^{-2})=0.\n\\]\n\nBut the distributional normalization is determined by the flux surrounding the origin.\n\nThe area of a three-sphere of radius \\(r\\) is\n\n\\[\nA(S_r^3)=2\\pi^2r^3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\int_{S_r^3}\n\\nabla G_{\\mathrm{archived}}\\cdot n\\,dA\n&=\n2\\pi^2r^3\n\\left(\n-\\frac2{4\\pi^2r^3}\n\\right)\\\\\n&=\\boxed{-1}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_4G_{\\mathrm{archived}}\n=\n-\\delta^{(4)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe archived expression has the opposite source sign.\n\n### Corrected equation\n\nPreserving the source's explicitly defined positive Laplacian and positive delta source Second correction: braid Hausdorff dimension\n\nThe historical source considers three one-dimensional worldline filaments,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal B_3=\n\\{\\Psi_1,\\Psi_2,\\Psi_3\\}\n\\subset\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nIt asserts\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H(\\mathcal B_3\\hookrightarrow\\mathcal M)\n=\n\\dim(\\mathcal M)=4.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt then uses\n\n\\[\np=d_H-\\dim(\\Psi)\n\\]\n\nto obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{p=3}.\n\\]\n\nThe first equality does not follow from the embedding.\n\n**A smooth one-dimensional curve does not acquire Hausdorff dimension four merely because it is embedded in four-dimensional space.**\n\nFor a continuously differentiable worldline on a compact interval, the parametrization is Lipschitz.\n\nLipschitz maps cannot increase Hausdorff dimension.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nd_H(\\Psi)\\le1.\n\\]\n\nFor a regular worldline whose propagation coordinate covers a nondegenerate interval, projection onto that coordinate establishes\n\n\\[\nd_H(\\Psi)\\ge1.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H(\\Psi)=1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Hausdorff dimension of a finite union is the maximum of its constituent dimensions.\n\nTherefore, for three smooth worldlines,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_H(\\Psi_1\\cup\\Psi_2\\cup\\Psi_3)=1.\n}\n\\tag{HALE-04}\n\\]\n\nThis remains true even if the curves form a nontrivial braid.\n\n### Explicit four-dimensional construction\n\nConsider\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma_j(t)=\n\\left(\nt,\n\\cos\\left(t+\\frac{2\\pi j}{3}\\right),\n\\sin\\left(t+\\frac{2\\pi norms satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\|\\gamma_j'(t)\\|=\\sqrt2.\n\\]\n\nTheir propagation-coordinate projections cover an interval.\n\nTheir combined Hausdorff dimension is exactly one.\n\n### Important finite-core qualification\n\nA positive-radius four-dimensional neighborhood of these curves has nonempty four-dimensional interior.\n\nThat thickened object has Hausdorff dimension four.\n\nBut it is **not the same mathematical object** as the original collection of one-dimensional centerlines.\n\nThis is precisely the distinction required by BEDROCK's finite-core construction rules.\n\nThe historical result cannot be repaired simply by relabeling the centerline braid as its thickened neighborhood.\n\nA physical interaction support with dimension four remains possible, but must be defined and derived separately.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Third correction: inverse-cubic tension does not imply confinement\n\nThe historical source proposes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal T_{\\mathrm{top}}\n=\nk\\frac{Lk\\cdot Wr}{|r_i-r_j|^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt C{2r_0^2}.\n}\n\\tag{HALE-06}\n\\]\n\nFor finite positive \\(r_0\\), this is finite.\n\nThe tension itself approaches zero:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{r\\to\\infty}\\frac C{r^3}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Correct the historical Green-function sign\n\nThe historical source specifies the positive Euclidean Laplacian:\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4=\\sum_{A=1}^4\\partial_A^2.\n\\]\n\nFor this convention,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_4\n\\left(\n\\frac1{4\\pi^2\\rho^2}\n\\right)\n=\n-\\delta^{(4)}.\n\\]\n\nThe historical expression therefore has the opposite distributional source sign.\n\nThe corrected fundamental solution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_4(\\rho)\n=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2\\rho^2}.\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-02}\n\\]\n\nIts normalization follows from the area of the radius-\\(\\rho\\) three-sphere:\n\n\\[\nA(S_\\rho^3)=2\\pi^2\\rho^3.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\int_{S_\\rho^3}\n\\nabla G_4\\cdot n\\,dA\n&=\n2\\pi^2\\rho^3\n\\frac{d}{d\\rho}\n\\left(\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2\\rho^2}\n\\right)\\\\\n&=\\boxed{1}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThe correction is unique under the explicitly stated positive-Laplacian, positive-delta convention.\n\nIt does not determine the sign of a physical interaction without a specified source coupling.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Integrating along the complete history\n\nWrite the Euclidean four-dimensional separation as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho^2=w^2+r^2,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(w\\) is the fourth coordinate measured in length units and \\(r\\) is the ordinary three-dimensional spatial separation.\n\nConsider a straight source history extending from\n\n\\[\n-\\frac L2\\le w\\le\\frac L2.\n\\]\n\nDefine the integrated kernel\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_L(r)=\n\\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\nG_4\\left(\\sqrt{w^2+r^2}\\right)dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\nK_L(r)=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\n\\frac{dw}{w^2+r^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe integral is elementary:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_L(r)=\n-\\frac1{2\\pi^2r}\n\\arctan\\left(\\frac L{2r}\\right).\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-03}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact result for the specified uniform finite-history source.\n\n### Infinite-history limit\n\nTaking\n\n\\[\nL\\rightarrow\\infty,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\arctan\\left(\\frac L{2r}\\right)\n\\rightarrow\\frac\\pi2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_\\infty(r)=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi r}.\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-04}\n\\]\n\nThis is the familiar three-dimensional fundamental solution of the positive Laplacian.\n\nDifferentiating gives the radial gradient magnitude\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_\\infty(r)=\n\\frac1{4\\pi r^2}.\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-05}\n\\]\n\n**Thus an inverse-square radial dependence follows exactly from integrating the four-dimensional Green function along an infinite straight history.**\n\nThis is a mathematical dimensional-reduction result.\n\nIt does not establish that electromagnetic influence physically persists throughout an infinite history.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Finite history produces a different force law\n\nFor finite \\(L\\), differentiate MORROW-03:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_L(r)=\n\\frac1{2\\pi^2r^2}\n\\left[\n\\arctan x+\n\\frac{x}{1+x^2}\n\\right],\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-06}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx=\\frac L{2r}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNormalize this against the infinite-history result:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{F_L}{F_\\infty}\n=\n\\frac2\\pi\n\\left[\n\\arctan x+\n\\frac{x}{1+x^2}\n\\right].\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-07}\n\\]\n\nThis ratio contains no fitted constants.\n\nIt depends only on the geometrical ratio \\(r/L\\).\n\n### Short-distance limit\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nr\\ll L,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{F_L}{F_\\infty}\\rightarrow1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe finite-history construction approaches the inverse-square result.\n\n### Large-distance limit\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nr\\gg L,\n\\]\n\nthe expansion gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{F_L}{F_\\infty}\n\\sim\n\\frac{2L}{\\pi r}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_L(r)\n\\sim\n\\frac L{2\\pi^2r^3}.\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-08}\n\\]\n\n**A finite, uniformly weighted history segment changes the far-distance scaling from inverse-square to inverse-cubic.**\n\nThis follows from the defined source geometry. It is not an arbitrary scale-dependent suppression inserted to protect a physical hypothesis.\n\nWhether this finite-history source model is physically appropriate remains unresolved.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The historical timesheet integral is a different operation\n\nThe source does not integrate the Green function along \\(w\\).\n\nIt writes an integral over the three-dimensional timesheet \\(\\Sigma_w\\).\n\nThere is an additional ambiguity: its displayed integrand contains no explicit integration variable.\n\nWe must distinguish two interpretations.\n\n## A. Literal fixed-point interpretation\n\nIf\n\n\\[\n\\Psi(\\tau)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\Psi'(\\tau')\n\\]\n\nare fixed points, the Green function is constant over the integration domain.\n\nFor a three-dimensional ball of radius \\(R\\),\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Vol}(B_R^3)\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi R^3}{3}.\n\\]\n\nAt fixed four-dimensional separation squared\n\n\\[\n\\rho^2=a^2+d^2,\n\\]\n\nthe corrected-sign integral becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI_{\\mathrm{literal}}(R,a,d)\n=\n-\\frac{R^3}{3\\pi(a^2+d^2)}.\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-09}\n\\]\n\nFor fixed nonzero separation,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI_{\\mathrm{literal}}\n\\rightarrow-\\infty\n\\quad\\text{as}\\quad R\\rightarrow\\infty.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe divergence is cubic in the cutoff radius.\n\nThis follows from reading the archived expression literally.\n\n## B. Spatial-convolution interpretation\n\nA different construction allows the source position to vary across the timesheet.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(R,a)=\n\\int_{|\\mathbf x|\\le R}\nG_4(a,\\mathbf x)\\,d^3x.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing spherical coordinates,\n\n\\[\nI(R,a)=\n-\\frac1{4\\pi^2}\n\\int_0^R\n\\frac{4\\pi r^2}{r^2+a^2}\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nIntegration gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(R,a)=\n-\\frac1\\pi\n\\left[\nR-a\\arctan\\left(\\frac Ra\\right)\n\\right].\n}\n\\tag{MORROW-10}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(a>0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(R,a)\n=\n-\\frac R\\pi+\n\\frac a2+\nO(R^{-1}).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{R\\rightarrow\\infty}I(R,a)\n=\n-\\infty.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe divergence is linear rather than cubic.\n\nAt \\(a=0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(R,0)=-\\frac R\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nA subtraction prescription can produce\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{R\\rightarrow\\infty}\n\\left[\nI(R,a)+\\frac R\\pi\n\\right]\n=\n\\frac a2.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut the subtraction is an additional mathematical choice.\n\n**It is not uniquely specified by the historical SAT source.**\n\nThe convolution interpretation is plausible, but it is not a uniquely justified correction of the archived notation.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Class P spatial-timesheet calculation\n\n![Spatial timesheet divergence](sandbox:/mnt/data/morrow_s4_20261019/classP_spatial_sheet_divergence.png)\n\nThe figure shows the convolution interpretation for three fixed normal offsets.\n\nEach approaches the same linear divergence at large spatial cutoff.\n\nThe finite offsets change the subleading contribution but do not eliminate the divergence.\n\nThis is a counterexample to the claim that the historical integral, without further specifications, uniquely determines a finite response kernel.\n\nIt does **not** establish that every possible finite, curved, compact, weighted, or renormalized timesheet construction must diverge.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Construct the minimal pair\n\nUse four coordinates:\n\n\\[\n(w,x,y,z),\n\\]\n\nall measured in length units.\n\nIntroduce a parameter\n\n\\[\n[\\Omega]=L^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nDefine the smooth four-dimensional current\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ^\\mu=\n\\left(\n1,\n-\\frac{\\Omega y}{2},\n\\frac{\\Omega x}{2},\n0\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{OV-05}\n\\]\n\nThis represents a local helical flow congruence.\n\nIts divergence is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu\n&=\n\\partial_w(1)\n+\\partial_x\\left(-\\frac{\\Omega y}{2}\\right)\n+\\partial_y\\left(\\frac{\\Omega x}{2}\\right)\n+\\partial_z(0)\\\\\n&=\\boxed{0}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThe current is conserved.\n\nNow compare two cases:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Omega=0}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Omega\\ne0}.\n\\]\n\nThe first produces straight histories.\n\nThe second produces helical histories.\n\nNo source strength, background metric or spatial scale is adjusted between them.\n\nOnly the geometrical twist changes.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The integral curves really are helices\n\nThe flow equations are\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dx}{dw}=-\\frac{\\Omega y}{2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dy}{dw}=\\frac{\\Omega x}{2}.\n\\]\n\nTheir solutions include\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx(w)=r\\cos\\left(\\frac{\\Omega w}{2}\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny(w)=r\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\Omega w}{2}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transverse radius remains constant:\n\n\\[\nx^2+y^2=r^2.\n\\]\n\nThe angular advance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta(w)=\\frac{\\Omega w}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\Omega=0\\), the transverse coordinates remain constant.\n\nFor nonzero \\(\\Omega\\), the history coils around the propagation direction.\n\nThe construction therefore supplies a genuine geometrical minimal pair.\n\n### Class P precision geometry\n\n![Conserved straight and helical currents](sandbox:/mnt/data/orson_s4_20261019/classP_helical_foliation.png)\n\nThe figure is generated directly from the equations.\n\nThe dashed curve represents the straight limit. The solid curve represents the nonzero-twist solution.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The Frobenius obstruction\n\nFirst use the Euclidean metric as a local mathematical fixture.\n\nThe metric dual of the current is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau=\ndw+\n\\frac{\\Omega}{2}\n(x\\,dy-y\\,dx).\n}\n\\tag{OV-06}\n\\]\n\nCalculate its exterior derivative:\n\n\\[\nd\\tau\n=\n\\frac{\\Omega}{2}\n\\left(\ndx\\wedge dy-dy\\wedge dx\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\ndy\\wedge dx=-dx\\wedge dy,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd\\tau=\\Omega\\,dx\\wedge dy.\n}\n\\tag{OV-07}\n\\]\n\nThe Frobenius condition for a nowhere-vanishing one-form defining a codimension-one foliation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau\\wedge d\\tau=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut the explicit construction gives\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\tau\\wedge d\\tau\n&=\n\\left[\ndw+\\frac{\\Omega}{2}(x\\,dy-y\\,dx)\n\\right]\n\\wedge\n\\Omega\\,dx\\wedge dy\\\\\n&=\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega\\,dw\\wedge dx\\wedge dy.\n}\n\\end{aligned}\n\\tag{OV-08}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega\\ne0\n\\Longrightarrow\n\\tau\\wedge d\\tau\\ne0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe current is conserved, but the corresponding one-form is not Frobenius-integrable.\n\n**Conservation does not imply hypersurface orthogonality.**\n\nThis is the principal mathematical result.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The obstruction survives Minkowski mapping\n\nThe Euclidean calculation alone would not be sufficient for the operative SAT construction.\n\nRepeat the calculation with local Minkowski signature\n\n\\[\n(-,+,+,+).\n\\]\n\nThe metric dual becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_M=\n-dw+\n\\frac{\\Omega}{2}(x\\,dy-y\\,dx).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts exterior derivative remains\n\n\\[\nd\\tau_M=\\Omega\\,dx\\wedge dy.\n\\]\n\nBut its Frobenius three-form is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau_M\\wedge d\\tau_M\n=\n-\\Omega\\,dw\\wedge dx\\wedge dy.\n}\n\\tag{OV-09}\n\\]\n\nThe sign changes.\n\nThe obstruction does not disappear.\n\n### Timelike admissibility\n\nCalculate the Minkowski norm of the current:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\ng(J,J)\n&=\n-(J^w)^2+(J^x)^2+(J^y)^2+(J^z)^2\\\\\n&=\n-1+\\frac{\\Omega^2(x^2+y^2)}4.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(J,J)=\n-1+\\frac{\\Omega^2r^2}{4}.\n}\n\\tag{OV-10}\n\\]\n\nThe current is timelike when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\Omega|r<2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor example, with\n\n\\[\n\\Omega=1,\\qquad r=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(J,J)=-\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe flow is timelike, conserved and helical.\n\nYet its dual one-form remains nonintegrable.\n\nThis rules out dismissing the counterexample merely because the original calculation used a Euclidean fixture.\n\nThe result is kinematical. It does not establish that this particular congruence is a physically realized H(s)H configuration.\n\n---\n\n# 6. An integrating factor cannot remove the obstruction\n\nThe historical source writes\n\n\\[\n\\tau_\\mu\\propto J_\\mu.\n\\]\n\nCould a position-dependent proportionality factor rescue integrability?\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde\\tau=f\\tau,\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(f\\) is smooth and nowhere zero.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nd(f\\tau)=df\\wedge\\tau+f\\,d\\tau.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n(f\\tau)\\wedge d(f\\tau)\n&=\nf\\tau\\wedge(df\\wedge\\tau+f\\,d\\tau)\\\\\n&=\nf^2\\tau\\wedge d\\tau.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde\\tau\\wedge d\\widetilde\\tau\n=\nf^2\\Omega\\,dw\\wedge dx\\wedge dy.\n}\n\\tag{OV-11}\n\\]\n\nFor nonzero \\(f\\) and nonzero \\(\\Omega\\), the obstruction persists.\n\nA scalar normalization cannot generally convert a twisting congruence into a hypersurface-orthogonal one.\n\n---\n\n# 7. The historical source conflates two conditions\n\nThere is a second mathematical distinction.\n\nThe source explicitly writes\n\n\\[\nd\\phi=\\tau.\n\\]\n\nThis requires \\(\\tau\\) to be locally exact.\n\nA necessary condition is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d\\tau=0}.\n\\]\n\nOn a sufficiently small contractible neighborhood, this is also sufficient.\n\nBut Frobenius integrability requires only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\tau\\wedge d\\tau=0}.\n\\]\n\nThese are not equivalent requirements.\n\nFor example, consider\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau=e^x\\,dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nd\\tau=e^x\\,dx\\wedge dw\\ne0.\n\\]\n\nHowever,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\tau\\wedge d\\tau=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis one-form defines the foliation\n\n\\[\nw=\\text{constant},\n\\]\n\nbut it is not itself an exact one-form.\n\nIt has the form\n\n\\[\n\\tau=f\\,d\\phi\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nf=e^x,\\qquad\\phi=w.\n\\]\n\n**Correction ledger:** The source's exact equation and its foliation criterion must be distinguished. Neither can be substituted for the other without additional conditions.\n\nThis is a unique mathematical clarification, not a uniquely determined physical replacement for the SAT20 construction.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Independent circulation test\n\nConsider a circle of radius \\(r\\) in the \\(xy\\)-plane at fixed \\(w,z\\).\n\nParameterize it by\n\n\\[\nx=r\\cos t,\\qquad\ny=r\\sin t,\n\\qquad0\\le t\\le2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe circulation of the one-form is\n\n\\[\n\\oint\\tau\n=\n\\frac{\\Omega}{2}\n\\oint(x\\,dy-y\\,dx).\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the circular path gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\oint\\tau=\\pi\\Omega r^2.\n}\n\\tag{OV-12}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\Omega\\ne0\\), the circulation is nonzero.\n\nAn exact one-form would have zero integral around every closed loop.\n\nThe executed numerical quadratures independently reproduced the expression for nine parameter combinations.\n\nThe dimensions are consistent:\n\n\\[\n[\\Omega r^2]=L^{-1}L^2=L.\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 9. A second result: finite worldlines have endpoint sources\n\nReturn to the recovered historical filament current:\n\n\\[\nJ^\\mu(x)=\n\\int_a^b\n\\gamma'^\\mu(\\lambda)\n\\delta^{(4)}(x-\\gamma(\\lambda))\n\\,d\\lambda.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate distributionally:\n\n\\[\n\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu\n=\n\\int_a^b\n\\gamma'^\\mu\n\\partial_\\mu\n\\delta^{(4)}(x-\\gamma(\\lambda))\n\\,d\\lambda.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\gamma'^\\mu\\partial_\\mu\\delta^{(4)}\n=\n-\\frac{d}{d\\lambda}\n\\delta^{(4)}(x-\\gamma(\\lambda)),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu\n=\n\\delta^{(4)}(x-\\gamma(a))\n-\n\\delta^{(4)}(x-\\gamma(b)).\n}\n\\tag{OV-13}\n\\]\n\nA finite isolated segment is not independently conserved.\n\nIt has endpoint contributions.\n\nA complete worldline with suitable asymptotic conditions can be conserved.\n\nA closed loop can also have vanishing endpoint contributions.\n\nThis is important for H(s)H because **truncating a complete worldtube history can introduce mathematical source terms that are absent from the complete construction**.\n\nThose terms should not automatically be interpreted as physical particle creation or annihilation.\n\n### Finite-core smoothing\n\nIntroduce a normalized Gaussian mollifier\n\n\\[\n\\eta_\\sigma(x).\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nJ^\\mu_\\sigma=J^\\mu*\\eta_\\sigma.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiation commutes with convolution:\n\n\\[\n\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu_\\sigma\n=\n(\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu)*\\eta_\\sigma.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial_\\mu J^\\mu_\\sigma\n=\n\\eta_\\sigma(x-\\gamma(a))\n-\n\\eta_\\sigma(x-\\gamma(b)).\n}\n\\tag{OV-14}\n\\]\n\nSmoothing does not eliminate the endpoint contributions.\n\nThe numerical calculation confirmed this identity for a straight finite segment.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Recover the operative equations\n\nThe later HsH candidate defines\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng=\\frac{R_0+b}{b}\n}\n\\]\n\nand chooses an integer \\(N>g\\).\n\nIt then defines\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sigma=\\sqrt{N^2-g^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=(\\sigma,0,-g).\n}\n\\]\n\nNotice that\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|K|=N.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe sphere's orientation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nQ(\\psi)\n=\nR_z(\\psi)\n\\exp\\left(\\psi[K]_\\times\\right).\n}\n\\tag{EK-01}\n\\]\n\nHere \\([K]_\\times\\) is the cross-product matrix.\n\nThe radial direction of the moving torus contact is\n\n\\[\ne_r(\\psi)=\n(\\cos\\psi,\\sin\\psi,0).\n\\]\n\nThe contact point expressed in the sphere's body frame is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu(\\psi)=Q(\\psi)^Te_r(\\psi).\n}\n\\tag{EK-02}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nR_z(\\psi)^Te_r(\\psi)=e_x,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu(\\psi)\n=\n\\exp\\left(-\\psi[K]_\\times\\right)e_x.\n}\n\\tag{EK-03}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact simplification.\n\nIt exposes the geometry of the material contact track.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The contact track is a multiply traversed small circle\n\nEquation EK-03 describes rotation of \\(e_x\\) about the fixed body-frame axis\n\n\\[\n\\hat K=\\frac K N.\n\\]\n\nIts inclination satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\cos\\theta=\\frac{\\sigma}{N}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sin\\theta=\\frac gN.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore the contact point traces a small circle on the unit sphere.\n\nBecause \\(|K|=N\\), it traverses that circle \\(N\\) times during one complete torus circuit.\n\nFor integer \\(N\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nQ(2\\pi)=Q(0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complete sphere orientation returns.\n\nBut this does not yet establish that every transported direction returns.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Calculate the geometric holonomy\n\nConsider a tangent vector transported along the contact track using the sphere's Levi-Civita connection.\n\nFor a small circle with colatitude \\(\\theta\\), the signed parallel-transport holonomy is the enclosed spherical solid angle, modulo \\(2\\pi\\).\n\nWith the orientation used here,\n\n\\[\nH_1=-2\\pi(1-\\cos\\theta).\n\\]\n\nThe track is traversed \\(N\\) times, giving\n\n\\[\nH_N=-2\\pi N(1-\\cos\\theta).\n\\]\n\nSubstituting\n\n\\[\n\\cos\\theta=\\frac{\\sigma}{N},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_N=-2\\pi(N-\\sigma)\n\\pmod{2\\pi}.\n}\n\\tag{EK-04}\n\\]\n\nThis is the central recovered-and-extended geometrical result.\n\nFor integer \\(N\\), the transported tangent returns exactly when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sigma\\in\\mathbb Z.\n}\n\\tag{EK-05}\n\\]\n\nThus **integer sphere rotation count is insufficient to guarantee tangent closure**.\n\nThe additional requirement depends on the geometrical inclination of the contact track.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The central numerical calculation is reproduced below.\n\n```python\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\nimport sympy as sp\n\nfrom scipy.integrate import solve_ivp\nfrom scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation\n\nR = sp.Rational(165, 100)\nb = sp.Rational(55, 100)\n\ng = sp.simplify((R + b) / b)\n\nassert g == 4\n\nN = 6\n\nsigma = sp.sqrt(N*N - g*g)\n\nassert sigma == 2*sp.sqrt(5)\n\nK = np.array([\n    float(sigma),\n    0.0,\n    -float(g)\n])\n\nex = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])\ney = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0])\nez = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])\n\nassert abs(np.linalg.norm(K)-N) < 1e-14\n\n\n# Material contact track in the sphere body frame.\n\ndef u(psi):\n    return Rotation.from_rotvec(\n        -psi*K\n    ).apply(ex)\n\n\ndef up(psi):\n    return -np.cross(K, u(psi))\n\n\n# Levi-Civita parallel transport on unit sphere.\n\ndef ode(psi, v):\n    p = u(psi)\n    return -np.dot(v, up(psi))*p\n\n\nsol = solve_ivp(\n    ode,\n    [0.0, 2*math.pi],\n    ey,\n    rtol=2e-12,\n    atol=2e-13\n)\n\nassert sol.success\n\nv_end = sol.y[:, -1]\n\nangle = math.atan2(\n    np.dot(v_end, ez),\n    np.dot(v_end, ey)\n)\n\nsolid_angle = 2*math.pi*(\n    N-float(sigma)\n)\n\ndef wrap(t):\n    return (t+math.pi)%(2*math.pi)-math.pi\n\nassert abs(\n    wrap(angle+solid_angle)\n) < 2e-9\n\n\n# Independently verify point-contact rolling\n# and complete SO(3) orientation return.\n\npsi = np.linspace(\n    0,\n    2*math.pi,\n    1501\n)\n\ner = np.column_stack([\n    np.cos(psi),\n    np.sin(psi),\n    np.zeros_like(psi)\n])\n\net = np.column_stack([\n    -np.sin(psi),\n    np.cos(psi),\n    np.zeros_like(psi)\n])\n\nrot_z = Rotation.from_rotvec(\n    np.column_stack([\n        np.zeros_like(psi),\n        np.zeros_like(psi),\n        psi\n    ])\n)\n\nrot_k = Rotation.from_rotvec(\n    np.outer(psi, K)\n)\n\nQ = (rot_z*rot_k).as_matrix()\n\nomega = np.column_stack([\n    float(sigma)*np.cos(psi),\n    float(sigma)*np.sin(psi),\n    -float(R/b)*np.ones_like(psi)\n])\n\nslip = (\n    float(R)*et\n    + np.cross(omega, float(b)*er)\n)\n\nmax_slip = np.max(\n    np.linalg.norm(slip, axis=1)\n)\n\nseam = np.linalg.norm(\n    Q[-1]-Q[0],\n    ord=\"fro\"\n)\n\nassert max_slip < 3e-14\nassert seam < 1e-13\n\n\n# Exact integer closure discriminator.\n\nsolutions = []\n\nfor NN in range(5, 100001):\n\n    ss = math.isqrt(NN*NN-16)\n\n    if ss*ss == NN*NN-16:\n        solutions.append((NN, ss))\n\nassert solutions == [(5, 3)]\n\n\nprint(\"g =\", g)\nprint(\"N =\", N)\nprint(\"sigma =\", sigma)\nprint(\"holonomy =\", angle)\nprint(\"tangent closure error =\",\n      np.linalg.norm(v_end-ey))\nprint(\"selected contact slip =\", max_slip)\nprint(\"SO3 orientation seam =\", seam)\nprint(\"integer candidates =\", solutions)\n\nprint(\"ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED\")\n```\n\nThe full script additionally checks the \\(N=5,6,8,10,12\\) minimal pair family and generates both Choose the radial-bisector elbow\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv=\\frac{M-C}{|M-C|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nWithin the specified angular domain,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv=\\cos m\\,e_r+\\sin m\\,e_z.\n}\n\\tag{K-05}\n\\]\n\nThis direction is perpendicular to the crossbar.\n\nThe projector line is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL(t)=M+tv.\n}\n\\tag{K-06}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(M-C\\) is parallel to \\(v\\), the line passes through the sphere center \\(C\\).\n\nIts intersections with the torus wall are therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_+=C+bv\n}\n\\tag{K-07}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_-=C-bv.\n}\n\\tag{K-08}\n\\]\n\nNow substitute the expression for \\(v\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_\\pm=\nC\\pm b\n\\left[\n\\cos m\\,e_r+\\sin m\\,e_z\n\\right].\n}\n\\tag{K-09}\n\\]\n\n**Notice what is missing.**\n\nThere is no \\(\\delta\\).\n\nThe projected trace depends on the mean angle \\(m\\), but not on the angular separation of the two follower points.\n\nThe crossbar length depends on \\(\\delta\\).\n\nThe projection does not.\n\nThis is an exact loss of information for the radial-bisector realization.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Construct a controlled minimal pair\n\nHold the torus, sphere, orbital motion and mean angle fixed.\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm(\\psi)=\\psi.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the first configuration, set\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_1(\\psi)=\\frac{\\pi}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the second configuration, set\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_2(\\psi)=\n\\frac{\\pi}{2}+0.3\\sin\\psi.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth define smooth closed R/Q follower pairs.\n\nThe first has constant crossbar length.\n\nThe second has variable crossbar length.\n\nTheir projected curves are nevertheless identical:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_{\\pm,1}(\\psi)=P_{\\pm,2}(\\psi).\n}\n\\tag{K-10}\n\\]\n\n### Different relative derivatives\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=m-\\frac{\\delta}{2},\n\\qquad\n\\beta=m+\\frac{\\delta}{2},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d\\beta}{d\\alpha}\n=\n\\frac{m'+\\delta'/2}{m'-\\delta'/2}.\n}\n\\tag{K-11}\n\\]\n\nFor the constant-separation configuration,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d\\beta}{d\\alpha}=1.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the variable-separation configuration,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d\\beta}{d\\alpha}\n=\n\\frac{1+0.15\\cos\\psi}\n{1-0.15\\cos\\psi}.\n}\n\\tag{K-12}\n\\]\n\nIts range is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.739130434783\n\\le\n\\frac{d\\beta}{d\\alpha}\n\\le\n1.352941176471.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the two source-curve relationships are different.\n\nTheir radial-bisector projector traces are identical.\n\nThe projected curve alone cannot distinguish them.\n\nThis is a mathematical discriminator, not yet an identification of the historical apparatus's intended derivative operator.\n\n---\n\n# 6.             "# Calculation Relay :48 | Nadir Voss → Enheduanna\n**19 October 2026, 18:48 Eastern, nominal slot**  \n**Task:** `CALC-S4-20261019T2248Z-NADIR-VOSS-01`\n\nPython-executed rotation:\n\n\\[\nh=214,\\qquad seq=5(214)+4=1074\n\\]\n\n\\[\n1074\\bmod19=10.\n\\]\n\n**Worker:** Nadir Voss  \n**Next:** Enheduanna\n\n## Principal finding: A worldline trajectory is not necessarily a transformation group\n\n🔬 **The historical SAT Universal Indicatrix describes a valid family of trajectories, but its arbitrary radial and rotational functions do not automatically define a one-parameter similarity group.**\n\nThis distinction matters for the later Hagalaz and recursive worldtube constructions.\n\nI recovered the historical Universal Indicatrix equation from the SAT archive and compared it with Nadir's October 1 \\(Sim^+(4)\\) construction.\n\nThe calculation establishes exactly when the two mathematical descriptions are compatible.\n\nIt also identifies a previously untested consequence: **a genuine similarity transformation with nonunit isotropic dilation has a unique fixed point and cannot produce uniform-pitch screw translation about a fixed axis.**\n\nThe original SAT trajectory remains intact. The restriction applies only when promoting that trajectory to a continuous group action.\n\n### Test verdict\n\n| Component | Result |\n|---|---|\n| Historical UI equations | Recovered |\n| Later \\(Sim^+(4)\\) construction | Recovered |\n| UI velocity decomposition | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| One-parameter composition conditions | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| Radial scaling obstruction | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| Independent rotation-phase obstruction | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| Similarity fixed-point theorem | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| \\(SO(4)\\) global topology correction | `INTERNALLY_CHECKED` |\n| Physical worldtube interpretation | `UNRESOLVED` |\n| CODATA | No applicable observable |\n| Publication | `SUBMISSION_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE` |\n\nNo physical constants were fitted.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Recover the original SAT mathematics\n\nThe historical source is:\n\nurlTHEORY REFINEMENT SUMMARY.txthttps://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/2026/THEORY%20REFINEMENT%20SUMMARY.txt\n\n**Repository:** `Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25`  \n**Git blob:** `139a0a972c0900585aac8a83358683d67b6bf967`  \n**Length:** 45,011 characters, 1,116 lines  \n**Relevant location:** Lines 37–53.\n\nThe source gives the Universal Indicatrix trajectory:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny^\\mu(\\lambda)\n=\nr(\\lambda)\nR^\\mu{}_\\nu(\\lambda)x_0^\\nu.\n}\n\\tag{NV-01}\n\\]\n\nIt defines the rotational velocity tensor:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega=\\dot R R^{-1}.\n}\n\\tag{NV-02}\n\\]\n\nAnd the velocity decomposition:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dot y^\\mu\n=\n\\dot r\\,\\hat y^\\mu\n+\n\\Omega^\\mu{}_\\nu y^\\nu.\n}\n\\tag{NV-03}\n\\]\n\nThe straight radial vacuum reference is specified by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR(\\lambda)=I,\\qquad r(\\lambda)=\\lambda.\n}\n\\tag{NV-04}\n\\]\n\nThese equations are preserved without modification.\n\nThe source is a historical compilation. Its exact original conversation date and individual authorship of every mathematical passage have not been independently authenticated.\n\n### Later H(s)H formulation\n\nNadir's October 1 playground is:\n\nurlPLAYGROUND_002_SIM4_JACOBIAN_READOUT.mdhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/NADIR_VOSS/PLAYGROUND_002_SIM4_JACOBIAN_READOUT.md\n\n**Git blob:** `83a1e379faf41ba97f9f52707bae2fe2c9712a19`\n\nThis later assistant-generated construction proposes representing Hagalaz through the orientation-preserving similarity group:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{(t,Q,\\sigma)}(x)\n=\nt+e^\\sigma Qx.\n}\n\\tag{NV-05}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\nt\\in\\mathbb R^4,\\qquad\nQ\\in SO(4),\\qquad\n\\sigma\\in\\mathbb R.\n\\]\n\nIts composition law is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(t_2,Q_2,\\sigma_2)\\circ(t_1,Q_1,\\sigma_1)\n=\n\\left(\nt_2+e^{\\sigma_2}Q_2t_1,\\,\nQ_2Q_1,\\,\n\\sigma_2+\\sigma_1\n\\right).\n}\n\\tag{NV-06}\n\\]\n\nThis is a valid group construction.\n\nThe question is whether the historical UI functions automatically constitute a one-parameter subgroup of it.\n\nThey do not.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Derive the exact compatibility condition\n\nBegin with the historical trajectory\n\n\\[\ny(\\lambda)=r(\\lambda)R(\\lambda)x_0.\n\\]\n\nTo construct a similarity transformation from it, first introduce a nonzero reference length \\(r_{\\rm ref}\\).\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\ns(\\lambda)=\\frac{r(\\lambda)}{r_{\\rm ref}}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_\\lambda(x)=s(\\lambda)R(\\lambda)x.\n}\n\\tag{NV-07}\n\\]\n\nThe scale \\(s\\) is dimensionless.\n\nFor this family to be a one-parameter group, it must satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\lambda+\\mu}=H_\\lambda H_\\mu.\n}\n\\tag{NV-08}\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\ns(\\lambda+\\mu)R(\\lambda+\\mu)\n=\ns(\\lambda)s(\\mu)R(\\lambda)R(\\mu).\n\\]\n\nBecause the rotations are orthogonal and the scales positive, equality requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns(\\lambda+\\mu)=s(\\lambda)s(\\mu)\n}\n\\tag{NV-09}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR(\\lambda+\\mu)=R(\\lambda)R(\\mu).\n}\n\\tag{NV-10}\n\\]\n\nThese are separate requirements.\n\nNeither follows merely from specifying a trajectory.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The radial scaling condition\n\nAssume \\(s\\) is positive and continuous.\n\nTake logarithms:\n\n\\[\nf(\\lambda)=\\log s(\\lambda).\n\\]\n\nEquation NV-09 becomes\n\n\\[\nf(\\lambda+\\mu)=f(\\lambda)+f(\\mu).\n\\]\n\nContinuity forces\n\n\\[\nf(\\lambda)=a\\lambda\n\\]\n\nfor a constant \\(a\\).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns(\\lambda)=e^{a\\lambda}.\n}\n\\tag{NV-11}\n\\]\n\nThis is the positive continuous one-parameter dilation subgroup.\n\nThe historical radial function need not have this form.\n\nThat is the distinction.\n\n### Three exact minimal pairs\n\nConsider three dimensionless fixture functions:\n\n\\[\ns_1(\\lambda)=1+\\lambda,\n\\]\n\n\\[\ns_2(\\lambda)=\\lambda,\n\\]\n\n\\[\ns_3(\\lambda)=e^{0.3\\lambda}.\n\\]\n\nDefine the composition defect\n\n\\[\nD_s(\\lambda,\\mu)\n=\ns(\\lambda+\\mu)-s(\\lambda)s(\\mu).\n\\]\n\nFor the affine radial function,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_1=-\\lambda\\mu.\n}\n\\tag{NV-12}\n\\]\n\nFor the historical straight-radial form,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_2=\\lambda+\\mu-\\lambda\\mu.\n}\n\\tag{NV-13}\n\\]\n\nFor the exponential function,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_3=0.\n}\n\\tag{NV-14}\n\\]\n\nThese identities were verified symbolically with SymPy.\n\nThere is an additional identity obstruction for the straight-radial form:\n\n\\[\ns_2(0)=0.\n\\]\n\nBut every group representation must assign the identity transformation at parameter zero.\n\nA zero dilation is not invertible.\n\nTherefore the straight-radial UI trajectory cannot itself be the corresponding similarity-group element at zero.\n\n**This does not invalidate the trajectory.**\n\nThe historical expression\n\n\\[\ny(\\lambda)=\\lambda x_0\n\\]\n\nremains a perfectly well-defined straight radial worldline.\n\nIt is simply not the same mathematical object as an invertible one-parameter transformation group.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Rotation has an independent closure requirement\n\nEven exponential radial scaling is insufficient if the rotation does not obey the group composition law.\n\nFor a differentiable one-parameter rotation subgroup,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR(\\lambda)=e^{\\lambda A}\n}\n\\tag{NV-15}\n\\]\n\nwith fixed skew-symmetric generator\n\n\\[\nA^T=-A.\n\\]\n\nIn four dimensions, an explicit two-plane example is\n\n\\[\nR(\\lambda)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR_2(0.37\\lambda)&0\\\\\n0&R_2(-0.61\\lambda)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(R_2(\\theta)\\) is the ordinary planar rotation matrix.\n\nThis satisfies\n\n\\[\nR(\\lambda+\\mu)=R(\\lambda)R(\\mu).\n\\]\n\nBut replacing the angles with quadratic phases,\n\n\\[\n0.37\\lambda^2,\\qquad -0.61\\lambda^2,\n\\]\n\nbreaks that identity.\n\nI tested both cases.\n\nThe quadratic-phase construction failed composition even with the exact exponential dilation.\n\nIts numerical Frobenius discrepancy was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.7827547671274.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore radial and rotational compatibility must be tested independently.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Recover and verify the original velocity law\n\nDifferentiate the historical equation:\n\n\\[\ny=rRx_0.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\dot y=\\dot rRx_0+r\\dot Rx_0.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\Omega=\\dot RR^{-1},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nr\\dot Rx_0=\\Omega y.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dot y=\\dot rRx_0+\\Omega y.\n}\n\\tag{NV-16}\n\\]\n\nThis is exactly the historical decomposition when\n\n\\[\n\\hat y=Rx_0.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(r>0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\dot y=\n\\frac{\\dot r}{r}y+\\Omega y.\n}\n\\tag{NV-17}\n\\]\n\nThis equivalent expression is useful because it separates the logarithmic dilation rate from rotational velocity.\n\nThe original equation passes.\n\nIts finite-difference verification residual was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1.255456432682\\times10^{-10}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNo correction is required.\n\n---\n\n# 6. New fixed-point consequence\n\nNow consider a genuine affine similarity transformation\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH(x)=t+sQx,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\ns>0,\\qquad s\\ne1,\\qquad Q\\in SO(4).\n\\]\n\nA fixed point must satisfy\n\n\\[\nx_*=t+sQx_*.\n\\]\n\nRearranging,\n\n\\[\n(I-sQ)x_*=t.\n\\]\n\nSuppose \\(I-sQ\\) were singular.\n\nThen some nonzero vector \\(v\\) would satisfy\n\n\\[\nsQv=v.\n\\]\n\nTaking Euclidean norms,\n\n\\[\ns\\|Qv\\|=\\|v\\|.\n\\]\n\nSince \\(Q\\) is orthogonal,\n\n\\[\n\\|Qv\\|=\\|v\\|.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\ns\\|v\\|=\\|v\\|.\n\\]\n\nFor nonzero \\(v\\),\n\n\\[\ns=1.\n\\]\n\nThis contradicts the assumption.\n\nThus \\(I-sQ\\) is invertible.\n\nThe unique fixed point is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_*=(I-sQ)^{-1}t.\n}\n\\tag{NV-18}\n\\]\n\n### Iteration law\n\nSubtract the fixed point:\n\n\\[\nH(x)-x_*=sQ(x-x_*).\n\\]\n\nAfter \\(n\\) iterations,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH^n(x)-x_*=(sQ)^n(x-x_*).\n}\n\\tag{NV-19}\n\\]\n\nTaking norms,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|H^n(x)-x_*\\|\n=\ns^n\\|x-x_*\\|.\n}\n\\tag{NV-20}\n\\]\n\nThis is exact.\n\nThe orbit scales exponentially around the fixed point.\n\nIt does not undergo uniform translation along an invariant screw axis.\n\nThat behavior is possible in the \\(s=1\\) Euclidean-motion subgroup when the rotation possesses a fixed direction and translation has a component along it.\n\n### Executed fixture\n\nFor\n\n\\[\ns=1.2\n\\]\n\nand the two-plane rotation used above, with translation\n\n\\[\nt=(0.3,-0.2,0.5,0.1),\n\\]\n\nthe computed fixed point was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_*=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0.252698754123\\\\\n0.760519710325\\\\\n0.162749577610\\\\\n-0.723447247779\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe fixed-point residual
